short: A creditor using AI must still give the specific, principal reasons for adverse action under ECOA and Regulation B, plus FCRA content when a consumer report or score was used. The CFPB withdrew its two AI circulars on May 12, 2025, but the law they explained is unchanged.
title: Adverse Action Notices for AI Underwriting
subtitle: What ECOA, Regulation B and the FCRA require when a model declines or prices credit, and what changed in 2025 and 2026
body_html:
A creditor that uses AI to decline or price credit must still tell the applicant the specific, principal reasons. That duty comes from the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and Regulation B, and a second notice duty comes from the Fair Credit Reporting Act when a consumer report or score played a part. The two CFPB circulars that spelled this out for AI were withdrawn on May 12, 2025. The statute and the regulation they explained were not changed.

Two laws, two sets of content, usually one letter

Under Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.9, a creditor must notify an applicant of adverse action within 30 days of receiving a completed application. The notice must give a statement of specific reasons, or tell the applicant of the right to request them within 60 days. The regulation says the reasons must be specific and indicate the principal reasons. It also says that pointing to internal standards or policies, or saying the applicant failed to achieve a qualifying score, is not enough.

Under section 615(a) of the FCRA, 15 U.S.C. 1681m, a separate notice is due when the action rests in whole or in part on a consumer report. It must name the consumer reporting agency, say that the agency did not make the decision, and explain the rights to a free copy of the report within 60 days and to dispute its accuracy. If a credit score was used, the notice must disclose the score and the key factors that hurt it. Most creditors combine both sets of content in one letter.

What AI changes, and what it does not

Nothing in either law mentions a model type, so the duty is the same for a scorecard and a neural network. What changes is how hard the duty is to meet. The official commentary to Regulation B says the reasons disclosed must relate to factors the system actually scored, and it does not prescribe one method for choosing them. A model with hundreds of inputs and interactions makes it harder to say which factors were principal for one applicant, and that difficulty is the creditor's problem to solve.

The withdrawn CFPB circulars

Circular 2022-03, issued May 26, 2022, said a creditor cannot use a complex algorithm when doing so means it cannot give specific and accurate reasons, and that not understanding your own model is no defense. It added that explanation methods applied after the fact only approximate a model, so the creditor must be able to validate them. Circular 2023-03, issued September 19, 2023, said a creditor may not lean on the checklist in the CFPB sample forms when those reasons do not reflect what actually drove the decision. Its example was a denial driven by the applicant's profession reported as insufficient income.

Both were among the 67 guidance documents the CFPB withdrew effective May 12, 2025. The Bureau said the withdrawal was not necessarily final and that the documents would not be enforced during its review. Do not cite them as current CFPB positions. They remain useful as a careful reading of rules that are still in force, and the Bureau is not the only enforcer: ECOA and the FCRA both give consumers a private right to sue.

The 2026 Regulation B rule did not touch the notice

On April 22, 2026 the CFPB published a final rule amending Regulation B, effective July 21, 2026. It removed the effects test and states that ECOA does not authorize disparate impact liability, narrowed the discouragement prohibition, and restricted special purpose credit programs. The adverse action notice provisions were left as they were. The National Consumer Law Center reports that a challenge to the rule is pending in federal court in the District of Columbia.

Building reason codes for a model

These steps follow from the rules above. They are our practical reading, not regulatory text.

  • List every input the model uses, including alternative data such as cash flow or rental history.
  • Pick a method for finding the principal factors for one decision, and test that it matches what the model really does.
  • Write a reason for each factor that a consumer can understand and act on. A reason that names a category is weaker than one that names the behavior.
  • Check that no reason is a stand in for internal policy or a bare score threshold, which Regulation B rules out.
  • When a consumer report or score is used, add the FCRA content and the score disclosure.
  • Keep the application and the notice for 25 months, as section 1002.12 requires for consumer credit.
  • If the model is a vendor's, get what you need by contract. The creditor, not the vendor, owes the notice.
